papers.title: Learning-informed uncertainty sets for maritime rerouting under strategic chokepoint disruptions
papers.title_zh: 战略咽喉中断下的学习型不确定集与海运改道
papers.boundary_note: Publisher exposes only the calendar date. The window starts at 2026-11-02 08:00 Asia/Singapore, so this is a boundary-day item: exact inclusion cannot be certified without a publication timestamp.
papers.version_status: Citable early peer-reviewed version; publisher states it may receive further edits before replacement by the final Version of Record.
papers.correction_status: Publisher record checked 2026-11-09; no separate correction or retraction relation observed.
papers.reading_scope: full_html_sections: publisher abstract, appendices, bibliographic/version/licence information and supplementary-file description; full equation layout and downloadable supplement were not independently downloaded; code not run.
papers.research_question: When route-condition forecasts feed cargo allocation and reserve decisions, do learned one-sided uncertainty widths improve disruption performance after holding the point forecast fixed?
papers.sample_clock_inclusion: Documented generated experiment with 396 route-quarter records for 18 generic alternatives in six corridor groups. Chronological blocks: 252 development, 72 calibration, 72 final evaluation; seven policies, six scenario transformations and four final quarters. Current outcomes are excluded from forecast features; advance signal is available one day before origin and lagged outcomes after the preceding quarter.
papers.core_method: For each adverse target k (delay, cost shock, capacity loss), construct an upper planning bound U^(k) = y_hat^(k) + w^(k), where the point forecast is shared and w is uniform, corridor-pattern or learned. Feed these bounds into a cargo-allocation/reserve-capacity optimization that minimizes evaluated generalized cost under fixed decisions and common realized scenarios.
evidence_anchors: publisher abstract with complete sample split and policy comparison
Appendix Tables 16–23: information timing, scenarios, chronological folds, marginal coverage and widths
Appendix Tables 24–25: seven cost components and file-to-stage joins
papers.principal_results: Relative to nominal optimization using the same learned point forecasts, learned widths reduce mean evaluated generalized cost by 30.67%. They nevertheless cost 3.54% more than uniform widths and 4.68% more than corridor-pattern widths. Final marginal coverage is 88.89% for delay, 81.94% for cost shock and 77.78% for capacity loss; fulfilled cargo is 97.28%, while only 30.72% is delivered within stated service thresholds.
papers.author_claim: Learned uncertainty can improve decisions relative to nominal planning, but need not beat simpler calibrated protection rules.
papers.independent_check: The strongest design feature is the controlled comparison: point forecasts and realizations are held common, isolating uncertainty-width construction. The evidence is still entirely generated, the nominal 90% target is missed for all three physical outcomes, and no observed shipping-market benefit is estimated.

papers.title: RAFT-ports: an application for risk assessment for tsunamis in ports demonstrated at Tanjung Gerem Port, Indonesia
papers.title_zh: RAFT-Ports：港口海啸损伤、损失与恢复评估工具
papers.correction_status: Publisher record checked 2026-11-09; no correction or retraction relation observed.
papers.reading_scope: full_html_sections: complete publisher HTML methods, results, limitations, data/code availability, Figures 2–7 descriptions and Table 1 summary; PDF not downloaded; repository endpoint was tested but returned 404; code not run.
papers.research_question: Can published depth-based fragility, loss and production-recovery functions be converted into an operational, reproducible port-level assessment workflow?
papers.sample_clock_inclusion: Tanjung Gerem Port, Indonesia; 430 buildings (346 chemical, 84 petrochemical) selected for multiple industry types, visible footprints, coastal proximity and prior inundation evidence. Three hypothetical Sunda Megathrust magnitudes (Mw 8.5, 8.7, 8.9), 100 stochastic slip realizations each; only the largest nearshore-amplitude realization per magnitude is carried into the detailed 5-hour, 5-m-grid demonstration.
papers.core_method: FUNWAVE–TVD propagates each selected tsunami through nested grids. For building b with representative inundation depth h_b, RAFT maps h_b to a 0.5-m depth bin and evaluates P(DS≥d | h_b), expected loss ratio E[L | h_b], and P(full production recovery by t | h_b). A user threshold τ (default 0.70) determines reported exceedances.
evidence_anchors: Methods: 300 slip models, five nested grids, 430-building inventory and independent QGIS/Excel replication
Table 1 and Results: thresholded damage, loss and recovery proportions
Scope and applicability: depth-only surrogate, topography resolution and transferability limitations
Code and Data Availability: claimed installers, source, samples and manual
papers.principal_results: At τ=0.70, 73%, 13% and 0% of structures in the Mw 8.9, 8.7 and 8.5 scenarios have at least a 70% probability of Minor-or-worse damage; 31%, 20% and 0% exceed the 70% expected-loss threshold. Some structures reach the selected recovery probability after about 2–2.5 months and all by 5–5.5 months. Independent replication gives identical probability calculations and ≤2.3% differences in depth-bin assignment.
papers.author_claim: RAFT-Ports operationalizes editable fragility and vulnerability functions for rapid scenario-based port impact and recovery assessment.
papers.independent_check: The innovation is implementation and traceability, not a new causal recovery model. Choosing the worst of 100 sources and using upper-bin depth is conservative locally, while coarse/raw terrain and transferring Tohoku-derived fragilities to Indonesia can bias in the opposite direction. The paper itself frames results as scenario impacts, not annualized risk.

papers.title: Mapping Future Energy Journeys Through Modeling the Global Transport of Synthetic Energy Carriers
papers.title_zh: 全球合成能源载体运输路径与基础设施选择
papers.correction_status: Publisher record checked 2026-11-09; no correction or retraction relation observed.
papers.reading_scope: full_html_sections: publisher abstract, introduction, methods, discussion/limitations, data and code availability and bibliographic record; source repository README/licence checked; model not run.
papers.research_question: Which combinations of production location, conversion chain and port/pipeline/shipping infrastructure minimize delivered costs for future synthetic energy carriers?
papers.sample_clock_inclusion: 10,883 production locations; destination countries Germany, Japan, China, India and the United States; seven Germany-focused scenarios in the main analysis; seven carriers and four transport modes; forward-looking 2030 techno-economic snapshot rather than observed trade flows.
papers.core_method: HERMES represents production, conversion and transport as a multi-commodity, multi-mode network. An iterative branching heuristic approximates a mixed-integer problem, minimizing delivered cost over eligible destination nodes, commodities, conversions and modes while pruning branches that violate benchmarks.
evidence_anchors: Figures/scenarios comparing retrofit, heat and commodity-value assumptions
Methods Eqs. 1–9 and iterative branch processing
Data/Code Availability: Zenodo data, source data, HERMES v1.0.0 and archived code
Discussion limitations: no port/ship capacity, congestion, loading, temporal operation or GHG accounting
papers.principal_results: Retrofit-ready pipelines keep moderate-renewable regions competitive; remote exporters depend strongly on ports and coastal pipeline access. Gaseous hydrogen dominates short pipeline paths, ammonia maritime paths, and methanol/methane longer multimodal chains. Low-cost heat is required for competitive LOHC routes. Results are scenario-dependent cost pathways, not observed trade forecasts.
papers.author_claim: Fine-resolution infrastructure and conversion representation changes which production regions and carriers appear cost-competitive.
papers.independent_check: The open model/data make the routing layer unusually auditable, but omission of port/ship capacities, fees, congestion and temporal occupancy means it cannot yet estimate operational disruption, AIS reorganization or emissions. It is a strong network-cost substrate, not a direct extreme-weather paper.

papers.title: Logistical competition and risk in wheat trade and impacts of changes in Black Sea shipping
papers.title_zh: 黑海航运变化下的小麦贸易、港口竞争与物流风险
papers.boundary_note: Publisher exposes only the calendar date. Because the search window starts at 08:00 Asia/Singapore on the same day, exact inclusion cannot be certified.
papers.correction_status: Publisher record checked 2026-11-09; no correction or retraction relation observed.
papers.reading_scope: full_html_sections: publisher abstract, model description, scenario results, conclusions, data availability and bibliographic record; downloadable PDF/code not obtained.
papers.research_question: How do seasonal port capacity, uncertain prices/freight/supply/demand and alternative Baltic/Caspian routes redistribute global wheat flows under Black Sea disruption?
papers.sample_clock_inclusion: Monthly global wheat-trade network with exporter ports and importing regions/countries; stochastic FOB prices, ocean freight, export supply, import demand and port capacity. The accessible HTML does not expose a concise complete estimation-period table or all input sample counts.
papers.core_method: Optimized Monte Carlo Simulation repeatedly solves a stochastic minimum-cost network-flow problem: minimize FOB plus ocean transport cost subject to monthly export supply, import demand, trade-policy and port-capacity constraints. Scenarios relax or expand Baltic/Caspian capacity and Russian export restrictions.
evidence_anchors: Model section: monthly stochastic network-flow design
Tables/scenarios: Baltic capacity and route changes
Conclusions: seasonal binding capacity and competing-exporter displacement
papers.principal_results: Base constraints bind mainly during peak seasons. A limited Baltic expansion shifts about 3.0 MMT; a larger expansion increases Baltic exports by 9.1 MMT while Black Sea/Sea of Azov exports fall 7.6 MMT. Relaxing the Russian export quota increases exports by about 2.4 MMT. The model predicts trade displacement across exporters and destinations, not only local port effects.
papers.author_claim: Seasonality, uncertainty and capacity constraints jointly determine route substitution, maritime-network resilience and trade competition.
papers.independent_check: The monthly capacity clock is a real advance over annual capacity comparisons. However, results depend on modeled costs/capacities and conflict scenarios; data are request-only, no public code was identified, and the model does not validate route changes against AIS.
